  MINUTES
  Regular Meeting
  ALHAMBRA CITY COUNCIL
  Council Chambers, 111 South First Street
  July 22, 2024
  6:00 p.m.
ROLL CALL: At 6:09 p.m., on Monday, July 22, 2024, the Alhambra City Council met in Council
Chambers of the Alhambra City Hall.

PRESENT:  LEE, MALONEY, PÉREZ, ANDRADE-STADLER, MAZA
ABSENT:  NONE

Officials Present: City Manager Binnquist, Assistant City Manager Garcia, Deputy City Manager
Hembree, City Attorney Montes, City Clerk Myles, Director of Parks and Recreation Macias, Director
of Library Services LohGuan, Chief of Police Kennedy, Chief of Fire Department Ragusa, Director of
Finance Lieu, Director of Human Resources Ko, Director of Community Development Ho, Interim
Director of Public Works and Utilities Ahlen, Principal Planner McCurley, Economic Development
Specialist Chew

FLAG SALUTE:  Led by Mayor Pérez

LAND ACKNOWLEDGEMENT: We acknowledge that the land on which we are gathered is the
traditional, ancestral, and unceded territory of the Gabrielino/Tongva peoples. We seek to prioritize
respect for the historic culture and contemporary presence of the native peoples throughout California,
especially in the greater Los Angeles/Alhambra area. We come with respect and gratitude for the
Gabrielino/Tongva people who still consider themselves the caretakers of this land. It is through their
examples that we are reminded of our greater responsibility to take care of Mother Earth and to take
care of each other.

CEREMONIAL

1.  COMMENDATIONS: ENVIRONMENTAL SCHOLARSHIP AWARD RECIPIENTS –
  F2M24-3

  Mayor PÉREZ and City Council wished to commend the recent winners of the Third
  Annual Environmental Scholarship Award. Republic Services joined with the City of
  Alhambra to award five scholarships of $1,000 to Alhambra students. Each finalist
  submitted an essay based on the theme of environmental stewardship and acknowledged
  the power of future generations to innovate greener living standards, an environmentally
  sound economy, and an environmentally sustainable lifestyle. The City of Alhambra was
  pleased to congratulate Alhambra students Cherry Ni, Kiara Cam and Sebastian Gonzalez
  for their achievements and for inspiring others through their dedication to the conservation
  of our planet. Mayor PÉREZ presented commendations to the scholarship award
  recipients.

PUBLIC HEARINGS

2.  CONSIDERATION  OF  AN  URGENCY  ORDINANCE  ENACTED  PURSUANT  TO
  1
7-22-24
   GOVERNMENT CODE SECTION 65858 EXTENDING A TEMPORARY MORATORIUM ON
  THE ISSUANCE OF PERMITS OR ENTITLEMENTS FOR ANY SELF-STORAGE PROJECT
  IN THE CITY – F2M23-7, N2M24-79, O2M24-4832, O2M23-4816, M2M24-111

  City Attorney MONTES delivered a staff report. At the July 24, 2023 City Council meeting, the
  City Council adopted an urgency ordinance placing a temporary moratorium on the issuance
  of permits or entitlements for any self-storage projects in the City, exempting two specific
  projects whose entitlements were already being processed by the City (2121 Orange and 1146
  South Meridian). On August 28, 2023, the City Council voted to extend the Moratorium, to be
  effective until July 22, 2024. The reasons for the moratorium and its first extension were set
  forth in Ordinance No. O2M23-4816. Staff prepared regulations governing the establishment
  of self-storage businesses and the Planning Commission made recommendations for some
  modifications. The Council considered the new regulations on June 24, 2024, made further
  modifications and introduced the ordinance for first reading. A second reading and possible
  adoption is scheduled for July 22, 2024. If adopted, the new regulations would take effect 40
  days later. The current moratorium will expire at the end of July 22, 2024, so a further extension
  is needed before any new regulations will take effect. The extension will last for an additional
  year, unless the new regulations are adopted, in which case the moratorium will expire on the
  date the new regulations go into effect. A report detailing the intended course of action by staff
  has been available in the City Clerk’s office since July 11, 2024.

  Opened & Closed the Public Hearing: Mayor PÉREZ opened the public hearing and as
  there was no one present who wished to speak, closed the same.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council took the following actions:

  1.  Conducted a public hearing.

  2.  Found that the recommended action is exempt from the California Environmental
  Quality Act ("CEQA") as set forth in the attached Urgency Ordinance (M2M24-111);
  and,

  3.  Adopted Ordinance No. O2M24-4832:

  AN URGENCY ORDINANCE OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF
  ALHAMBRA, CALIFORNIA, ENACTED PURSUANT TO CALIFORNIA
  GOVERNMENT CODE SECTION 65858, EXTENDING A TEMPORARY
  MORATORIUM ON THE ISSUANCE OF PERMITS OR ENTITLEMENTS FOR
  ANY SELF-STORAGE PROJECT IN THE CITY

  which ordinance went into effect immediately extending Ordinance No. O2M23-4816
  for a period of one year, unless regulations governing self-storage projects were
  adopted sooner.

  Vote:  Moved:  MALONEY  Seconded:  ANDRADE-STADLER
  Ayes:  LEE, MAZA, MALONEY, ANDRADE-STADLER, PÉREZ
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

3.  CONSIDERATION OF AN URGENCY INTERIM ZONING ORDINANCE EXTENDING
  ORDINANCE NO. O2M23-4818, THE PROHIBITION ON THE ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW
  FIREARMS SALES BUSINESSES AND DETERMINE THIS ACTION IS EXEMPT FROM
  2
7-22-24
   CEQA – F2M23-7, N2M24-80, O2M24-4833, O2M23-4818, M2M24-128

  City Attorney MONTES delivered a staff report. At the September 25, 2023 City Council
  meeting, the City Council adopted an urgency ordinance placing a temporary moratorium
  prohibiting the establishment of new firearm sales businesses in the City. (“Moratorium”). On
  October 23, 2023, the City Council voted to extend the Moratorium, to be effective until
  September 24, 2024. The reasons for the moratorium and its first extension were set forth in
  Ordinance No. O2M23-4818. Staff continued to work on permanent regulations, and
  continued to monitor legislation and pending litigation as to the enforceability of potential
  regulations. Staff anticipated bringing forward a buffer ordinance that would limit the
  establishment of new retail firearm sales businesses in areas near sensitive uses. In the
  meantime, given the duration of the moratorium, staff also recommended that the moratorium
  not apply to the relocation of existing businesses within the City, provided that any such
  business is not proposing to expand its business. The current moratorium would expire at the
  end of September 24, 2024. The extension would last for an additional year until and through
  July 22, 2025, unless new regulations are adopted. A report detailing the intended course of
  action by staff was available in the City Clerk’s office since July 11, 2024.

  Mr. MONTES noted two corrections needed to be made pertaining to “Recommended Action
  No. 3” listed on the agenda referencing the title of the Urgency Ordinance and Section 2 of the
  ordinance itself. He noted in both instances the corrections were to replace incorrect language
  referring to self-storage projects and replace that language with language pertaining to firearm
  sales in the City.

  Opened & Closed the Public Hearing: Mayor PÉREZ opened the public hearing and as
  there was no one present who wished to speak, closed the same.

  Discussion: Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER and Mr. MONTES discussed an
  existing firearms business, Euro Arms, Inc., that had operated in the City of Alhambra since
  1989 and were in the process of relocating. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER and Mr. MONTES went
  on to discuss the “buffer zones” for firearm retailers and how this business would be affected
  as an established business. Director of Community Development HO provided clarity as to the
  new location of the business in question.

  Councilmember MAZA motioned to approve the Urgency Ordinance, which was seconded by
  Vice Mayor LEE. The motion failed due to a vote of 3/4 [AYES: LEE, MAZA, MALONEY;
  NOES: ANDRADE-STADLER] and 1 abstention [PÉREZ]. A 4/5 vote was required to adopt
  the urgency ordinance.

  Mr. MAZA made a second motion to reconsider the item, which was seconded by Ms. LEE.
  The motion passed due to a vote of 5/5 [AYES: LEE, MAZA, MALONEY, ANDRADE-
  STADLER, PÉREZ]. Mr. MAZA discussed the history of Euro Arms, Inc., their upstanding
  record of business, their connection to the Police Department, and stated that there would not
  be any new issues in their new location. He expressed that it was unfair to subject an existing
  business after 36 years of business. He stated that the business had discreet signage, tinted
  windows, and limited clientele.

  Mr. MAZA made a third motion to approve the urgency ordinance, which was seconded by
  Ms. LEE. The third motion passed with a vote of 4/5.

  Action Taken:  City Council took the following actions:

  1.  Conducted a public hearing.

  2.  Found that the recommended action was exempt from the California Environmental

  and,

  3.  Adopted Ordinance No. O2M24-4833 by a 4/5 vote:

  AN URGENCY ORDINANCE OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF
  ALHAMBRA, CALIFORNIA, ENACTED PURSUANT TO CALIFORNIA
  GOVERNMENT CODE SECTION 65858, EXTENDING A TEMPORARY

  firearms sales businesses were adopted sooner.

4.  PUBLIC HEARING TO ADOPT RESOLUTION NO. R2M24-28 APPROVING GENERAL
PLAN MAP AMENDMENT AMD-23-06, PLANNED DEVELOPMENT PERMIT PD-23-  43,
PLANNED DEVELOPMENT PERMIT PD-23-44, PLANNED DEVELOPMENT  PERMIT PD-
23-45, CONDITIONAL USE PERMIT CUP-23-19, CONDITIONAL USE  PERMIT CUP-23-20,
TENTATIVE PARCEL MAP TPM-23-02, MITIGATED NEGATIVE  DECLARATION,  AND
MITIGATION MONITORING AND REPORTING PROGRAM, AND AN ORDINANCE O2M24-
4834 APPROVING  ZONING MAP AMENDMENT AMD-23-05, AT  146 SOUTH PALM
AVENUE (APN: 5342-022-033 & APN: 5342-022-035), 127 SOUTH RAYMOND AVENUE (APN:
5342-022-034), 132 SOUTH PALM AVENUE (APN: 5342-022-  036), 2018 TEAGARDEN
LANE (APN: 5342-022-053), AND 126 SOUTH PALM AVENUE  (APN:  5342-022-054)  –
F2M24-50, N2M24-81, O2M24-4834, R2M24-28

  This was the time and place set by Notice No. N2M24-81 for the City Council to hold a public
  hearing to consider an application for the proposed Palm and Pepper Commercial
  Development which would consist of three (3) drive-through, quick-serve food-related uses (a
  Starbucks®, a Raising Cane’s®, and a Panda Express®) totaling 7,053 square feet of floor
  area located within a 2.7-acre site consisting of four (4) parcels. Principal Planner Maia
  McCURLEY delivered a staff report and presentation, which is on file in the City Clerk’s office.
  The project requested a General Plan Map Amendment to change the General Plan land use
  classification from Industrial to General Commercial, and a Zoning Map Amendment to change
  the Zoning classification from I (Industrial) to CMU (Commercial Mixed-Use) to facilitate the
  proposed development. Additionally, the project requested approval of applications for
  Planned Development Permits, Conditional Use Permits, and a Tentative Parcel Map. A
  Mitigated Negative Declaration (MND) as well as a Mitigation Monitoring and Reporting
  Program (MMRP) were prepared for the project. Due to the project’s requirement for a Zoning
  Map Amendment and General Plan Map Amendment, the City Council was the final
  decision-making body for all of the project’s associated applications and environmental
  documents. On June 3, 2024, the Planning Commission voted 5-1 to adopt Resolution No.
  24-11 recommending the City Council approve the proposed project’s applications along with
  the Mitigated Negative Declaration (MND) and Mitigation Monitoring and Reporting Program
  (MMRP) prepared for the project. An in-depth description and analysis of each application
  associated with the proposed project was provided in the Planning Commission Staff Report
  from June 3, 2024 (Attachment 6 of staff’s July 22, 2024 report). The City Council was now
  asked to consider final approval of the various applications outlined in the title of this agenda
  4
7-22-24
   item. As part of the consideration of the project applications, the City Council would also
  consider the specific recommendations provided by the Planning Commission. The Planning
  Commission incorporated five (5) additional conditions of approval related to the re-zoning of
  adjacent properties and modifications to the site design. Finally, pursuant to the California
  Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), an Initial Study and Mitigated Negative Declaration was
  prepared for the project. The findings of the Initial Study were that the proposed project would
  result in less than significant impacts with the incorporation of mitigation measures. The
  specific mitigation measures were discussed in detail in the Initial Study – Mitigated Negative
  Declaration (Attachment 4, Exhibit C of staff’s July 22, 2024 report) and in the Mitigation
  Monitoring and Reporting Program (Attachment 4, Exhibit D of staff’s July 22, 2024 report).
  Ms. McCURLEY elaborated on the Planning Commission recommendations and the additional
  recommendations made by staff.

  Open public hearing: Mayor PÉREZ opened the public hearing.

  Public Comment:  Lewis McCAMMON, 105 N. Cordova St., spoke in support of the
  project and staff recommendations on the Planning Commission’s recommendations. He went
  on to discuss the traffic in the area specifically related to Costco and expressed hope that the
  traffic queuing would not imitate the In-and-Out drive through on Garfield Ave. Mr. McCammon
  also referred to a handout pertaining to Item No. 44 regarding the lack of housing and
  specifically low-income housing. He added that while this area could be zoned for housing, he
  supported the proposed project. He further discussed Item No. 12 as it may relate to the
  proposed project.

  Close public hearing:  After receiving public comment, Mayor PÉREZ closed the public
  hearing.

  Discussion: Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER spoke in support of the project and the
  work conducted by staff to help develop it. She supported the Planning Commission
  recommendation No. 2 to consider site plan revisions to include pedestrian
  interconnectedness on site and further recommended the installation of bike racks. She also
  supported staff recommendations regarding No. 4 due to the fact that repositioning the location
  of the two buildings would reduce drive-thru queueing length. She also supported Planning
  Commission recommendation No. 5 to reconsider the plant palette to include larger native
  trees for the site.

  Councilmember MALONEY and Ms. McCURLEY discussed the existing inholding properties
  at 128 S. Palm and 117 S. Raymond Ave. Ms. McCURLEY explained that there were no
  business licenses, zoning clearance, or occupancy permits for an active business on file for
  128 S. Palm. She stated that 117 S. Raymond Ave. was a recent building with a current active
  occupant. She further explained these locations would still be able to operate as office space
  under the proposed zoning change to Commercial Mixed Use.

  Mr. MALONEY and Ms. MCCURLEY further discussed the Mitigated Negative Declaration and
  the mitigation measures. Ms. McCURLEY explained the reasons for the Negative
  Declarations. They continued to discuss the Planning Commission recommendation No. 3
  regarding a redesign of the public right-of-way to include a parkway with trees. Ms.
  McCURLEY explained staff’s argument against this recommendation due to the fact that there
  was no current long-term plan for the smaller streets at this area to obtain a right of way width
  during development projects that would allow for certain improvements such as parkways,
  sidewalks, or additional lanes. She added that it was premature to do these improvements for
  individual potential developments without a long-term plan to thoroughly connect them. She
  clarified that the proposed development on Pepper Street proposed to re-landscape the
  perimeter of the property as part of their landscape plan to include native plants, which would
  serve as a parkway type space. Mr. MALONEY and Ms. McCURLEY continued to discuss the
  5
7-22-24
   trees and plants proposed, and Mr. MALONEY encouraged the developer and staff to utilize
  truly California native species rather than species that have been introduced to California. They
  continued to discuss the plants selected.

  Mr. MALONEY and Ms. McCURLEY further discussed the proposed Starbucks. Mr.
  MALONEY stated that he would prefer a design which allowed for outdoor seating. He also
  supported Ms. Andrade-Stadler’s suggestion to include bike racks. He ultimately supported
  the project.

  Councilmember MAZA spoke in support of the project as it would improve the area from its
  current use. He stated that he supported staff recommendations regarding recommendations
  No. 3 and 4, in terms of the landscaping design and the driveway queue, and supported Mr.
  Maloney’s suggestions regarding Recommendation No. 5 and use of California Native plants.

  Vice Mayor LEE commented on the traffic in the area of the proposed project and supported
  measures to control traffic flow. Ms. LEE and Ms. McCURLEY discussed existing Starbucks
  locations in the City as well as the new proposed location in the project. She commented on
  the discrepancy between Planning Commission recommendations and staff recommendations
  and expressed discomfort with choosing between the recommendations. She stated that a
  compromise ought to have been reached prior to Council review. She went on to discuss the
  recommendations with Ms. McCURLEY and reiterated staff’s reasoning for their
  recommendations as well as the discussions with Planning Commission. They continued to
  discuss recommendations No. 3 and 4. Ms. LEE stated that her main concern was traffic
  mitigation and supported staff’s determination regarding recommendations 3 and 4.

  Mayor PÉREZ noted the trend for repeat businesses in the City and listed the other locations
  of the proposed businesses in the project. Ms. PÉREZ and Mr. HO discussed staff’s process
  to attract new businesses during discussions with developers. Mr. HO stated that the majority
  of the time, property owners make financial choices based on their best interests despite the
  interests of the community. He further elaborated on staff’s efforts to request new businesses
  and the shared vision of the community. Ms. PÉREZ echoed Mr. Maloney’s comments
  regarding the Starbucks and its lack of seating. She expressed her preference to create more
  spaces for people to sit down rather than focus on expanding parking. She discussed the
  opportunity to make different designs furthering the City’s goals to increase walkability. She
  referred to Mr. McCammon’s comments regarding the need for more affordable housing. She
  stated that this was a missed opportunity to utilize the space and continued to discuss the
  need to move away from car focused developments. Mr. HO stated that staff was in agreement
  with Council’s vision but added that this was an automobile centered area of the City given the
  other developments and that creating a more pedestrian focused development in the area may
  have additional concerns. He also discussed the decline of commercial industrial properties in
  the area and the proposals that are presented to the City. Ms. PÉREZ reiterated her points
  and her desire to emphasize the City’s overall vision for a more pedestrian friendly community.

  Ms. McCURLEY further addressed Mr. MALONEY’s comments regarding the Negative
  Declaration for air quality and the mitigation efforts. She clarified that this pertained to the
  construction phase of the project and that the mitigation efforts consisted of sweeping the site,
  removing dust, watering to contain dust, and offering contact information for the contractor
  and project manager.

  Mr. MALONEY motioned to direct staff to include Planning Commission recommendations 1,
  2, and 5 with a focus on California native trees, follow staff’s analysis regarding Planning
  Commission recommendations 3 and 4, to adopt the Resolution, and give first reading to the
  Ordinance. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER seconded the motion.

  Action Taken:  City Council:

PRESENTATIONS

5.  APPROVAL OF UTILITY BOX PUBLIC ART AT THE SOUTHWEST CORNER OF WEST
  MAIN AND SOUTH FIRST STREETS – F2M24-16, M2M24-112

  Economic Development Specialist Tiffany CHEW delivered a staff report and presentation,
  which is on file in the City Clerk’s office. The Alhambra Central Business District Association
  and City staff worked with local business Nucleus Gallery to develop a public art opportunity
  at a utility box in the Downtown. The purpose of the public art was foster community pride and
  reflect the Alhambra Community. The public art would also be appropriate for the entire
  community to view and complement adjacent buildings and businesses. A utility box at the
  7
7-22-24
   southwest corner of West Main and South First Streets was identified as a location for the
  public art project. This utility box was owned by the City and would add public art to the
  Downtown street intersection. The Arts & Cultural Events Commission reviewed the proposed
  artwork at their May 15, 2024 meeting and they supported the project and provided positive
  input on the design and composition.

  Discussion: Vice Mayor LEE discussed the proposed artwork, the recommendation from
  the Arts & Cultural Events Commission, and the Art in Public Places fund. Councilmember
  ANDRADE-STADLER discussed the past Council direction to staff in developing public art
  projects throughout each district. Ms. LEE continued to discuss the funding source for the
  project and the progress of the Arts Commission to produce art for each district with Director
  of Parks and Recreation MACIAS. Mr. MACIAS clarified that this utility box public art was
  separate from the allocated $10,000 for each district. Director of Community Development HO
  clarified the selection of this utility box by the Alhambra Downtown Business Association. Ms.
  LEE continued to discuss the subject matter and design for the utility box in terms of inclusivity,
  representation from other cultures, and use of public dollars for broader public appeal.
  Councilmember MAZA noted that this was one box and that the other utility box projects would
  display other art styles. He motioned for approval. Councilmember MALONEY also spoke to
  the subject matter of the design and stated that the dragon figure was represented in many
  other cultures. He seconded the motion. Mayor PÉREZ supported the design and the artists
  selected by Gallery Nucleus. She continued to speak in support of continuing this program.

  Action Taken: City Council approved the utility box public art at the southwest corner of West
  Main and South First Streets; appropriated funds in the amount of $800 from the Public Art
  Fund; and, directed staff to undertake the steps necessary to finalize Council’s action. (
  M2M24-112)

  Vote:  Moved:  MAZA  Seconded:  MALONEY
  Ayes:  MALONEY, MAZA, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE, PÉREZ
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:NONE

6.  DECISION APPROVAL AND NOTICE INVITING BIDS FOR THE PURCHASE OF
  ALHAMBRA PLACEMAKING SIGNAGE – F2M24-51, F2M24-33, N2M24-89, M2M24-114

  Director of Parks and Recreation MACIAS delivered a staff report and presentation which is
  on file in the City Clerk’s office. As part of the adopted 2024 Strategic Plan, staff worked with
  the Arts & Cultural Events Commission to discuss “Place Making Centers” throughout the City.
  Staff recommended placement at three park locations. The suggested locations were Granada
  Park, Alhambra Park, and Almansor Park. On June 19, 2024, the Arts & Cultural Events
  Commission approved the “Alhambra” placemaking signs to be a part of a photo opportunity
  campaign throughout the City. These signs would be created to inspire residents and visitors
  to visit various Alhambra sites. People would be encouraged to snap a picture and post it on
  social media, enjoy a picnic, or take in the views. The signs would be approximately 16 feet
  long by 8 feet tall. Specifications and bid documentation were completed for the Alhambra
  Placemaking Sign Project.

  Discussion: Vice Mayor LEE and Mr. MACIAS discussed the design of the signs, the
  placement of markers at other parks, and the estimated cost of the signs. Councilmember
  ANDRADE-STADLER and Mr. MACIAS spoke regarding the placement of the signs with
  regard to safety. Councilmember MAZA and Mr. MACIAS discussed the placement of the sign
  at Almansor Park and suggested reaching out to residents and historical records to see
  examples of script used in past welcome pamphlets for Alhambra. They went on to discuss
  the material used in the construction of the signage. Councilmember MALONEY and Mr.
  8
7-22-24
   MACIAS discussed the Notice Inviting Bids, the approval process by the Arts & Cultural Events
  Commission, and taking inspiration from other sources in Alhambra. Mayor PÉREZ supported
  the signage for Granada Park and Mr. Maza’s suggestion to refer to past pamphlets for
  inspiration.

  Action Taken: City Council approved the design concept; authorized the circulation of a

  undertake the steps necessary to finalize the Council’s action. (M2M24-114)

7.  APPOINTMENTS TO THE 710 TERMINUS REGIONAL PLANNING TASK FORCE PER SB
  710 (DURAZO) – F2M23-19, M2M24-118

  Assistant City Manager GARCIA delivered a staff report. On June 26, 2024, the City received
  notice of Caltrans and Senator Durazo’s intent to kick off the 710 Terminus Regional Planning
  Task Force. Pursuant to SB 710 (Durazo), the bill required the establishment of a Task Force
  for the purposes of completing a report to the California Legislature on the issues of traffic and
  potential land use related to the State Route 710 Terminus adjacent areas, as defined. The
  Task Force, which included representatives from Alhambra, Los Angeles (90032), the County
  of Los Angeles, Cal State University Los Angeles, Los Angeles County Metropolitan
  Transportation Authority, a business or workforce entity, a community-based organization, and
  Caltrans, were to meet on a quarterly basis. By December 1, 2025, the Task Force would
  complete and submit a report to the Legislature, and provide an update on Alhambra’s 710
  Arterial Project. As part of the process, community engagement was expected. Based on

  F2M20-24, O2M24-4831

  After receiving staff’s presentation and public testimony at the June 24, 2024 public hearing,
  the City Council deliberated and determined which of the Planning Commission’s
  recommendations to include and gave first reading to Ordinance No. O2M24-4831 approving
  a Zone Text Amendment amending various sections of the Alhambra Municipal Code on
  zoning, as well as adding new sections, to address new State legislation and clarify ambiguous
  provisions as well as correct typographical and formatting errors and modify use allowances.
  At its February 26, 2024 meeting, the City Council adopted Ordinance No. O2M24-4828, which
  proposed minor changes to the AMC to reflect current practices, clarify confusing parts of the
  AMC, and bring outdated sections into compliance with State law. This ordinance was brought
  separately from Ordinance No. O2M24-4828 because it proposed changes to the City’s Zoning
  Code, which required review by the City’s Planning Commission. This proposed clean-up
  addressed items that were identified in the lead-up to and shortly after the January 22, 2024
  adoption and March 2, 2024 implementation of the comprehensive Zoning Code update,
  including addressing new State legislation, eliminating inconsistencies, and creating greater
  clarity in implementing the new Zoning Code. The various items addressed in this Municipal
  Code clean-up fell within two (2) broad categories: 1.) proposed amendments and 2.) proposed
  additions. All of the proposed amendments and additions have been reviewed for consistency
  with the City’s General Plan, as required by AMC Section 23.33.080 (General Plan
  Consistency Required for Zoning Amendments).

  The City reviewed the environmental impacts of the proposed ordinance under the California
  Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq. “CEQA”) and the
  regulations promulgated thereunder (14 Cal. Code of Regs. §§ 15000, et seq., the “CEQA
  Guidelines”). This Ordinance was not subject to further review environmental review because:
  (1) it would not result in a direct or reasonably foreseeable indirect physical change in the
  environment (14 Cal. Code Regs. § 15060(c)(2); (2) there was no possibility that this
  Ordinance would have a significant effect on the environment (14 Cal. Code Regs. §
  15061(b)(3)); and (3) the Ordinance, by itself, did not constitute a “project” as defined in section
  21065 of the Public Resources Code and the CEQA Guidelines (14 Cal. Code Regs. § 15378).
  It could be seen with certainty that there was no possibility that this Ordinance may have a
  significant effect on the environment. Staff requested that the City Council introduce O2M24-
  4831 for its second reading and adopt the ordinance.
